question: A 10-year-old boy with acute kidney injury has serum K 7.2 mEq/L. The ECG shows peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex. Which of the following is the FIRST drug to administer?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sodium bicarbonate shifts potassium into cells (useful in acidosis), but it does not act on the cardiac membrane. When ECG changes are present (peaked T waves, widened QRS), the immediate priority is membrane stabilisation with calcium gluconate — cardiac protection comes before redistribution.

Insulin-dextrose is a highly effective potassium-lowering measure (shifts K into cells within 15–30 minutes), but it does not protect the myocardium from the immediate risk of arrhythmia. Calcium gluconate must be given first to stabilise the cardiac membrane when ECG changes are present.

Correct. Calcium gluconate (10%, 0.5–1 mL/kg IV over 5–10 minutes, with cardiac monitoring) is the first-line drug when hyperkalaemia produces ECG changes. It acts within minutes to antagonise the effect of hyperkalaemia on the cardiac membrane (membrane stabilisation), buying time for potassium-lowering measures such as insulin-dextrose, sodium bicarbonate, and Kayexalate.

Nebulised salbutamol (a beta-2 agonist) redistributes potassium into cells and can lower serum K by 0.5–1.0 mEq/L, but it is an adjunctive measure, not first-line when life-threatening ECG changes (widened QRS) are present. Calcium gluconate is always given first for membrane stabilisation.

overallFeedback.feedback: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, calcium gluconate is the first drug — it stabilises the cardiac membrane within minutes. Potassium-shifting agents (insulin-dextrose, NaHCO3, salbutamol) and removal strategies come next. The order matters: membrane protection first, then redistribution.

Correct. The management sequence for symptomatic hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is: (1) membrane stabilisation with calcium gluconate → (2) shift K into cells (insulin-dextrose, sodium bicarbonate, salbutamol) → (3) remove K from the body (diuretics, Kayexalate, dialysis).
